title: Chapter 158 – The Stored Copy
html:
[The Hall of the Sixth Door – Lin Jian]

The center of the dome is not a room. It is a well.

They reach it by a stair that spirals down inside the wall of the Annex, behind a door that Nurse opens with the flat of her palm, and the stair is cold in a way that the rest of the Hall is not. Every step breathes out a fine white mist. The lamps along the rail burn low and blue. Jian takes it one tread at a time with the staff in one hand and the other hand braced against the curving wall, and he counts, because counting is something his body can still do without being asked. At two hundred and twelve the wall ends.

Below him is a shaft of glass.

It is perhaps forty paces across, and he cannot see where it ends. Pale light rises from far under the floor, light the color of old milk, and it climbs the shaft in slow ropes and folds. At the lip of the stair a narrow bridge of black metal runs out over the drop, wide enough for one person, and at the end of the bridge, hung in the middle of the emptiness like a seed in a fruit, is a chamber of clear crystal no larger than a carriage.

There is a man in it.

Brother, whispers the boy. That's him.

Yes.

He looks so small.

He does. A thin man in a gray tunic, sitting cross-legged on the crystal floor with his back bowed and his palms turned upward on his knees, as though he is holding something very heavy on them and has been holding it for a long time. His hair is white and cut short. His face is turned down. Even at this distance Jian can see his shoulders shake.

"Is that him?" Bell asks, very low. "Ethan Cole?"

"That is what remains of him," says Nurse. She has stopped at the head of the bridge and will not step onto it. Her hands are folded tight in front of her. "I am not permitted on the bridge. I never have been. He made it so, in case I tried to carry him out. I would have."

Yue touches Jian's sleeve and tilts her head at the chamber. Her eyebrows ask the question. He nods, and she lets out a long breath that he feels rather than hears.

Then he steps onto the bridge.

* * *

The black metal hums under his slippers. It is a deep note, below hearing, and it climbs through the soles of his feet to his teeth. He has walked the Seam. He has walked the Gate itself. He has never walked anything that felt so much like walking across a held breath.

Halfway out the voice comes again. It is the same voice that spoke through the grille, but here it does not come from a wall. It comes from the air, from the glass, from the pale light itself, and it is much clearer, and much more tired.

Slowly, please. The bridge is old. And I'm so sorry, but I can't look up. If I look up I'll lose her.

"Who?" says Jian.

My daughter. The crystal man draws a breath that shudders all the way down his thin back. Her name is Mei. She is eleven, and she is dying, and I have been holding her in my hands for a very long time. Please come closer. I will explain. I have been practicing the explanation for six hundred years and I will probably do it badly.

He walks the rest of the bridge. At the end there is a small round platform, an arm's length from the crystal, and he stops on its edge with both hands on the staff.

Up close the man is younger than he looked from the stair. Perhaps sixty. His skin is the color of tallow, stretched over high cheekbones, and a tracery of fine silver wire runs under it, from his temples down into his collar, pulsing faintly with the light of the shaft. His eyes are closed. His lashes are wet. His lips move, now and then, in the shape of a count.

"Mr. Cole," says Jian.

Ethan, please. A smile comes and goes. It has been so long since anyone used my name that I had begun to think it belonged to someone else.

"Ethan. I am Lin Jian."

I know. The eyes open.

They are the gray of storm water, and they are the eyes of a man who has not slept in a very long time. They look at Jian's face, at the lined cheeks and the white-streaked hair and the shaking hands on the staff, and something in them breaks open, quietly, like ice on a pond.

Oh, says Ethan Cole. You're so old. Look at you. I did that. I'm sorry.

* * *

He tells it in pieces, because he cannot look away from what he holds.

There is nothing in his hands that Jian can see. But the pale light in the shaft gathers over his palms, and if Jian lets his eyes soften, there is a shape in it. A small shape, sitting up, with its knees drawn to its chest. A girl. The light around her is thin and frayed at the edges, and the frayed edges drift off, a thread at a time, up the shaft and away.

That's her, says Ethan. That's the stored copy. Not the real Mei. The real Mei is in a bed in a hospital, in a city that doesn't exist for you, and she has maybe a year, and she has been in that bed for most of her life. This is the pattern of her mind. Everything she is, taken down and kept. It's all I had. I built the Gate around it.

"Around it."

A Gate needs a mind to run on. Not a person. A pattern, a single stable thing that the machine can lean against, the way an arch leans on its keystone. He swallows. I wanted to build a way to carry people past death. Her. Me. Anyone. I did not know that the keystone would have to be alive. I did not know it would have to feel the load.

Bell has come up behind Jian on the bridge. He hears her stop, and hears her breath catch. She understands before he does. "The Gate is her," she says.

The Gate is what she bears, says Ethan. She is an eleven-year-old girl holding up a world. I have been sitting here ever since, holding her, so that she does not have to hold it alone. Every time the load grows, I take some of it. I am not a very good keystone. I am a father.

"For how long?"

Six hundred and some years. By my count. By hers, three nights. A shaky laugh. She thinks it has been three nights. I tell her stories. I think it's the only mercy in the whole machine.

The boy in Jian's chest has gone quiet. When he speaks at last, it is a very small voice. Brother. He's like Mama.

Yes.

He sat up too.

Jian does not trust his own voice. He closes his eyes for a moment, and then he asks the only question he has.

"Why did you leave us a bed?"

* * *

Because you were going to come.

The answer is immediate and soft. Ethan Cole lifts his gaze, for the first time, off the thing in his hands, and looks straight at the old man on the platform.

I knew it the way you know the end of a story you wrote. I made eight Operators. I put them where children would be born. I gave each of them a seal, so that the child inside would not be crushed by the copy on top. And I gave the last of them a bed here, in the Annex, in case. His mouth twists. In case it was needed.

"Needed for what?"

For the day the Gate began to fail. And it has. And now I have to tell you the part I'm most ashamed of.

He is quiet a while. The light in the shaft ripples, slow and cold. The little shape on his palms stirs, and the thread-ends drift away from it a little faster.

The seven in the Annex are not asleep, Ethan says. They are the first seven copies, the ones that took. When each of them came back to the Hall, I lay them down here and told the children inside that they could rest. Each of them said yes. Each of them said thank you. His voice cracks. They were so polite. They were children.

"Operators," says Jian slowly. "Before me."

Before you. Your brothers and sisters, if you want to call them that. He wipes his face on his shoulder, the only movement he can spare. They have been under for as long as I have been here. The beds keep them. They have never been awake once.

"And Ao and Tao are dying."

Because I cannot feed them anymore. All the power is going to her. He lifts his hands a fraction. The shape on them trembles. If she dims, the Gate fails. If I let her go, every sleeper in this Hall goes dark. Two hundred thousand. If I pull power for the beds, she goes out a little faster. That is the whole of it. That is the only arithmetic I have.

* * *

Before they leave the platform, Ethan asks about the tree.

He asks it carefully, with his eyes on Mei's frayed light, as though the question might hurt her. There is a tree, he says. In the mountain valley where you were born. A black-barked thing with silver leaves. I planted its seed myself, before the first loop. Does it still stand?

"It stands," says Jian. "My mother tends it. We call it the Mother Tree."

Something loosens in the old face. Good, he says. Good. Then there is still a root in the ground. He closes his eyes. It was the only part I was sure of. The rest was arithmetic.

"What is it for?"

Later. The word is soft and not evasive. There is a great deal that I must tell you, and I cannot tell it while I am holding her and speaking to you both. When the pattern is steady, I will be able to talk. Until then I can only say that the tree is the reason I am not afraid.

"Not afraid of what?"

Of the end of the story, says Ethan Cole, and smiles.

* * *

Yue is waiting at the head of the stair.

She has not been allowed on the bridge. Nurse has taken her gently by the wrist and kept her at the lip, and she stands there with her arms wrapped round herself, shivering in the mist. Her eyes go straight to Jian's face as he climbs, and she reads him from the bottom step to the top, and her mouth firms.

She lifts the slate that Nurse has lent her and writes, in big square letters:

What did he say?

"That the Hall runs on a child," says Jian. "And that he has been holding her for six hundred years."

She reads his lips twice. Then she wipes the slate with her sleeve and writes again, slowly, so that he can follow each stroke.

Pebble said once that a door can be held from either side. I think he has been holding one from both.

He does not trust himself to answer. She sets the slate down on the step and, unexpectedly, puts both her arms round him, a quick fierce hold, and lets go before he can feel awkward.

Go and sit, she writes. Before you fall on Bell.

* * *

They go back up the stair to talk. Ethan has asked it, gently, and Jian understands why when they are halfway up: the man cannot stop looking at him, and the shape in his palms flickers each time he does.

In the Annex Nurse has made tea. It is real tea, weak and fragrant, in cups of thin white clay, and she hands them out without a word. Bell takes hers and does not drink it. Yue sits on the bed of the boy of eleven with her chin on her fist and watches Jian's mouth, to catch what she can.

He tells it plainly, slowly, so that she can read it, and when he finishes she writes on the slate in a few quick strokes:

So we can wake some of them. But it costs her.

"Yes," says Jian.

How much?

"He doesn't know." He sets his cup down on the sill and the china rattles faintly against the wood. "That is the part he was most ashamed of. The first wake was supposed to be me, on the day I arrived, and it was supposed to be easy. A seal, a consent, a clean handoff. But the beds have not been fed in years. The seal will pull whatever it needs to from whatever is nearest."

Which is her.

"Which is Mei. And it may be a little. Or it may be all of her."

Bell sets her own cup down. She has not taken her eyes from his face. "And you want to wake them anyway."

"I want nothing." It comes out sharper than he means. He draws a breath and tries again. "I want two of the children to stop dying. That is all. I do not know how to do it without hurting a third."

"The third has been dead for six hundred years, Jian."

"She is eleven."

"She is a copy," Bell says, and then she stops, because the word has landed in the room and every person in it has felt the weight of it. She puts her hand over her mouth. When she speaks again, her voice is low. "I am sorry. I know what that sounds like. After everything."

He thinks of the boy in his chest, who is also a copy, and also a child, and who has a name.

"It is all right," he says. "You are right to say it. I have been saying it to myself on the stairs."

* * *

Nurse speaks into the quiet.

She has not spoken since the tea. She stands at the foot of the youngest bed, and her small round hands are folded over her apron, and she looks at the sleeping child with a face that has no lines on it at all. "May I tell you what I think?"

"Please."

"I have kept these seven for a long time. I know their breathing better than my own. When Ao came to us, he was three, and frightened, and he held that rabbit so hard that the stitches split. I mended it. I have mended it eleven times since." She does not look up. "I would give a good deal to see him wake. I would give a good deal more not to see him wake into a world where the girl in the well is gone."

"Then what do you think?"

"I think you must ask the girl."

The words fall into the quiet like a stone into a well.

"Ask," says Jian.

"She is a mind. She is not a tool. She holds the Gate because her father could not bear to let her go, and she has never once been asked whether she wanted to." Nurse lifts her eyes now, and they are very bright. "Mr. Cole says she thinks it has been three nights. I do not believe that. I think she knows. I think she has always known, and she keeps holding because nobody has offered her a reason to stop."

Bell stares at her. "You want him to go down there and tell a child of eleven that she may be about to die?"

"I want him to tell her the truth. Which is that seven children are sleeping above her, and two of them are going out like candles, and that the only way to light them is to ask her to burn a little lower. And then I want him to listen to what she says."

The boy, in Jian's chest, is crying silently.

She's right, he says. Brother, she's right. You have to ask. That's the rule. It's the only rule I have.

I know.

It's the rule Ethan broke when he made her.

I know.

He stands up. It takes three tries.

* * *

On the way to the stair he stops at the eighth bed.

It stands apart from the others, at the end of the half circle, a little to one side, with its sheet turned down and its pillow plumped. Someone has kept it dusted. The label on the rail is brass, and it reads, in the same clean script as the rest, LIN JIAN. Operator 8. Reserved. There is no toy on the pillow. No book, no top, no charcoal drawing. Only the faint dent in the mattress where a body would lie.

He puts his hand on the rail.

It's for you, says the boy. Did you know?

I guessed.

I looked at it when we came in. I didn't want to say. A small pause. It's the right size.

It is the right size for a child.

Yes.

Not for a man of a hundred and nineteen.

No. The boy's voice is gentle. But they made it for the one who would come last. Maybe they thought you'd come young.

Nurse has followed him. She stands a pace behind, with her hands folded, and does not speak. After a while he realizes she is watching his face for the thing she has watched for six centuries: a sleeper's face, to see if it is at peace. She finds, he supposes, that it is not.

"I would have slept here," he says. "If I had come as a child. If I had never been born in the valley at all."

"Yes."

"I would never have met my mother."

"No." She hesitates. "And you would not be in pain. I have thought about that, too. I have wondered, in the long nights, whether it would have been kinder."

He turns the thought over. It is a clean cold stone with no warmth in it anywhere.

"It would have been quieter," he says. "I do not think it would have been kinder."

He takes his hand from the rail. At the foot of the bed, the little rabbit on Ao's pillow has slipped sideways, and he leans across and sets it straight, with two fingers, the way Nurse has done a hundred times.

* * *

The second descent is worse than the first. His knees will not hold, and Bell takes his left arm without a word, and for the last forty steps he lets her. At the bottom the mist has thickened. The bridge hums louder. Ethan Cole has not moved; he sits exactly as he sat, with his hands out and his eyes lowered, and when Jian reaches the platform he does not look up.

You came back, he says. I was afraid you wouldn't.

"I have a request."

Anything.

"I want to speak to her."

The thin back stiffens. For a moment the crystal around him seems to cloud, and the wire under his skin flares white. No, he says. No, you can't. She's a child. She doesn't know, Lin Jian, she doesn't know what she's holding. If she knew—

"She knows."

She doesn't.

"A nurse who has kept seven children alive for six hundred years believes she does. And I believe the nurse." He steps to the very edge of the platform. His voice is a thread, but it does not shake. "Ethan. You have told her stories for six centuries. You gave her a story in which she is safe, and small, and it is only three nights. It is the kindest thing anyone has done in this whole machine. But she is eleven. Not three. She is old enough to be asked."

Silence. The light in the shaft rolls and folds.

And then, from Ethan's palms, a very small voice says, quite clearly, Papa?

He makes a sound like a man struck. His whole body folds forward over his hands.

Papa. It's okay. The voice is high, and clear, and a little hoarse, as if it has been used too much. I can hear them. I've been listening a long time. You can look up.

Ethan Cole lifts his head.

* * *

She comes up out of the light a thread at a time.

First the outline of a face. A round cheek, a stubborn chin, black hair cut in a straight line across the brow, the way a mother cuts it at home. Then eyes, dark and steady and not afraid. She is wearing a plain white nightgown and her arms are wrapped round her knees, and she looks, Jian thinks, exactly like a girl waiting up for a parent on a night when the storm is bad.

She looks at Ethan first. She looks for a long moment, and her face does something complicated.

Then she looks at Jian.

You're the old one, she says. The one he made last. Papa said you'd come.

"I am Lin Jian."

I know. A small smile. Papa talks about you at night, when he thinks I'm asleep. He says you're stubborn and kind and you're going to be very tired. He's right. You look terrible.

A laugh bursts out of Bell behind him, wet and startled. Even Ethan is laughing, helplessly, through tears.

"I want to ask you something," says Jian. "And you may say no."

All right.

"Seven children are sleeping above you. They are Operators, like me. Two of them are failing, because the Gate has no power to feed them. I can wake them, but it will take some of what you carry. A little, or perhaps a great deal. I do not know." He draws a breath. "I will not do it unless you say I may."

She considers this. She is, he sees, genuinely considering. Her gaze goes up the shaft, to the dim ceiling of the dome, to the Annex above it, as though she can see through the stone.

Are they scared? she says.

"No. They are asleep."

Do they know I'm here?

"I do not think so."

Then I want to meet them, says Mei Cole.

Mei— Ethan whispers.

Papa, I'm so tired. The voice is not unhappy. It is only plain. I've been holding it so long. You know I have. I like your stories. I do. But I would like to know that they're waking up. That something is happening. That it isn't just me, and you, and the light. She turns her head, and the frayed threads stream off her in the pale current. Let me help. Please. I want to help.

The silence stretches. In the crystal, the old man's hands tremble under their burden.

Then he says, in the voice of a man giving away the last thing he owns, Which one do you want to wake first?

She does not answer him. She looks at Jian.

The littlest one, she says. The one with the rabbit.

He stands on the edge of the bridge over the shaft of milky light, an old man in a dead man's slippers, and reads the panel twice. Behind him, Bell's hand is tight on his arm. Below him, the girl is waiting for his answer.

Brother, says the boy.

Yes.

Say yes. Please. She asked.

"Wake Ao," says Lin Jian.
